title: Every licensing misstatement found and fixed, enforced by a grep verifier

the_licence.why_it_matters: PolyForm Shield carries a Noncompete clause and a Competition clause that counts goods and services as competing even when provided free of charge. Telling a reader the project is open source or MIT-licensed tells them they hold rights the licence withholds, and the correction lands after they have committed.

corrections.now: Free to download, source-available. Windows, macOS, Linux. Vulkan / DX12 ready.

corrections.note: "owned by the community" carried no banned phrase but was the same false promise: PolyForm Shield does not transfer ownership. Corrected in the same sentence.

publish_slint_checkbox_decision.what_it_is: A choice a creator makes about their own Space when publishing it, not a statement about Eustress.
publish_slint_checkbox_decision.reasoning: The checkbox attaches no licence to anything. A creator who ticks a box labelled "Open Source" on a platform that is not open source can reasonably believe they have applied an OSI licence they never chose. The helper text beside it already said the true thing — "Allow source access and reuse" — so the label was the only part that overclaimed. It now reads "Share Source", which is what the control does.
publish_slint_checkbox_decision.identifier_rename: The bound property spellings were changed from open-source to open_source in the same pass. Slint normalises identifiers (i-slint-compiler parser.rs::normalize_identifier maps foo_bar to foo-bar), so the two spellings are the same identifier and the generated Rust accessors are unchanged. No Rust call site, no publish-manifest field, and no serialised name was touched.

scope_extensions.note: Two edits fall outside the item's declared in-scope file list. Both are recorded here rather than made quietly. Each is a one-line revert.

entries.why_out_of_scope: The item's in-scope list names eustress/crates/web/src/pages/ and style/main.css, not the crate's index.html.
entries.why_it_was_fixed_anyway: The line is a machine-readable licence declaration in the live site's schema.org JSON-LD: "license": "https://opensource.org/licenses/MIT". Search engines and open-source programme-office scanners read that field directly. It is the single most consequential misstatement found, and it is a false MIT claim rather than a phrasing slip. The item's own measurement missed it because a grep for "open source" and "open-source" does not match "opensource.org". Leaving it would have meant either suppressing a real defect or reporting zero while a false MIT claim stayed live.
entries.revert: git checkout -- eustress/crates/web/index.html (note: this file also carries the founder's uncommitted edits)

entries.why_out_of_scope: The file is on neither the in-scope nor the out-of-scope list.
entries.why_it_was_fixed_anyway: Section 13 lists third-party projects (VS Code, Monaco, Zed, Lapce, pulldown-cmark) as architecture references. "Third-Party References" is what the section actually contains, and the retitle is accurate on its own terms rather than a licence edit.

not_touched.LICENSE: Changing the licence to match a description is a human-only decision. This item only changed descriptions to match the licence, which alters no terms.
not_touched.third_party_licence_descriptions: Statements about MinIO, fbxcel, the Autodesk FBX SDK and the rojo-rbx crates are true as written and were left alone. They are carried on the allowlist.
not_touched.deployment: The corrected tree is left in place. Publishing the site and deploying to production are human-only.
not_touched.founder_uncommitted_work: The working tree carried 91 uncommitted paths before this item and 91 after. The baseline measurement runs under `git stash`, which converts five staged deletions into unstaged ones; they were re-staged afterwards and `git status --porcelain` now matches the pre-item snapshot exactly.

pdf_regeneration.why: The PDF is generated from the HTML and is the file that actually gets emailed. Correcting only the HTML would leave a wrong PDF in the tree.
pdf_regeneration.generator_of_record: The committed PDF's /Creator field reads HeadlessChrome/147.0.0.0, so the same pipeline was used.
pdf_regeneration.verifier_cannot_read_pdfs: The verifier skips PDFs exactly as `grep -I` does. An early draft inflated FlateDecode streams and it was removed: the only text it recovered from the marketing PDFs was embedded-font metadata (Monotype Arial ships a Biblical-Hebrew layout notice that says "open source software under the MIT License"), which is noise about a font vendor and not about Eustress. The sha256 pair above is the evidence that the PDF was regenerated, not a grep.
pdf_regeneration.visual_confirmation: The regenerated PDF was rendered and read page by page. The header tag reads "SOURCE-AVAILABLE · PHYSICS-AS-CODE · BUILT FOR INVENTORS", step 01 reads "Free to download, source-available.", the CTA reads "Help shape the source-available platform of the future for inventors. Built in the open, and every line of it is yours to read, fork and build on.", and the footer reads "Source-available (PolyForm Shield 1.0.0) · Read, fork and build on it · Git-diffable projects · No vendor lock-in".

verifier_design_notes.scan_universe: The whole repository from --repo-root down. 6,315 text files scanned. Binary files are skipped the way `grep -I` skips them.
verifier_design_notes.why_not_a_file_list: A scanner pointed at the files the author already found cannot catch the next occurrence, which is the entire point of leaving it behind. The baseline run proves it: it independently found five further misstatements in eustress/crates/web/index.html (:10, :24, :35, :67, :103, all claiming "open source" and "Apache-2.0") that the item's own catalogue never listed.
verifier_design_notes.rule_statement_classification: Three lines outside docs/PROMPTS state the house rule itself — 'say "source-available", never "open source"'. They are classified out, not allowlisted, on the same ground the prompt library itself is excluded: text that quotes the phrase in order to forbid it is not a claim. The test is same-line only — the correct term must appear on the very line that carries the banned phrase — and every line set aside is printed and stored verbatim in the report.
verifier_design_notes.allowlist_durability: Entries match on path + line + exact text. Edit the line and the entry stops matching, so the hit resurfaces for a fresh decision instead of staying suppressed forever.
verifier_design_notes.ci_readiness: The checker exits 0 clean, 5 on unallowlisted hits, 6 on an allowlist violation, 7 on a missing or too-small baseline. A later item can wire it into CI as-is; it needs nothing but python and a repo root.
